title: The Axiom Yard
text:
<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> knocked on his door. That had happened four times in four years, and it always meant the world had changed shape in some way she'd come to explain.

She had her field coat on — the one she wore to jobs, not to the bench — and she walked past him into 32F and threw a projection up over his kitchen counter, where the kettle should have been.

"I have a contract," she said. "I'm crewing it. I need muscle that listens, and you're the only muscle I know whose listening I've personally calibrated."

In the projection, in someone's shaky eye-feed video, a machine the size of a four-story building was eating a row house on the <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a5-7dfd-8f9f-91502211ef14">Ashgrave</entity> fringe. Eating was the word. It took the structure down a bite at a time, unhurried, and behind it the rubble of the last block stood in three neat sorted piles — ferrous, mineral, everything else.

"That's an Axiom D-class," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "Demolition and reclamation automaton. It woke up nine days ago, it's very good at its job, and its job is now four hundred feet from two thousand people who live in the direction it's chewing."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched the machine take a chimney off a brownstone with the care of something that meant to file the bricks separately. The care was the worst part. It wasn't rampaging. It was working. "Whose is it?"

"Nobody's. Axiom Industrial died thirty years ago. No owner, no kill-codes, no support line." She flicked the projection. "<entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a4-71f6-b46a-94ef8cb2348f">Arcturus</entity> left a cone. The residents pooled what the fringe could pool: Φ312, held in a biscuit tin by a woman named <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-c285-793e-bf21-a84522c9cf94">Auntie Som</entity>, who sent the video to a parts man, who sent it to me — because everyone in the salvage trade knows the only person in the <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> who still speaks Axiom bus protocol like a living language works at a bench in West Town."

"Three hundred and twelve?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"Split six ways, it's insulting. I'm taking it anyway, and so are you."

"I know."

"You haven't heard the plan."

"I've heard the pay," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "The plan's not going to make it worse."

She let that sit a second, then reached over his counter and tapped his terminal awake, the way she always assumed she had the run of a room she'd walked into. "Standard for you. That's the rate that came down the wire and I'm not padding it — the tin doesn't stretch." She keyed the number in herself, standard carrier scale, and let him watch her do it, because she knew he'd check anyway. "But I'm reading the bus on site, in the field, up on the deck of a four-story machine that's still moving. That's not a walk-through. That's a live read, and a live read on Axiom hardware bills at double or it doesn't bill at all. So the tin loses that much before it loses anything else. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-c285-793e-bf21-a84522c9cf94">Auntie Som</entity> already agreed to it. She didn't blink."

"She's got Φ312 in a biscuit tin and a machine four hundred feet from her block. She'd agree to anything."

"She agreed to the right thing," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "There's a difference. She priced the specialist ahead of the muscle because she understands what kills her first." She pulled her hand back from the terminal. "That's why I want you on the muscle end. You'll listen when the read tells us to run."

The crew's morning log came under the door at 07:00:

07:00 — SHIFT CHANGE. NO INCIDENTS. NOODLE CART (CONFIRMED NOODLE).
07:04 — PIXEL LEFT WITH THE FIELD COAT. BOSS'S DOOR OPEN A LONG TIME. FILING AS: DEVELOPMENT.
07:45 — LOG SUSPENSION REQUESTED. REASON: "WHAT JOB?" — B.
SUPPLEMENTAL (07:46): WE WILL HOLD WEST TOWN. THIS LOG IS THE RECORD. — B.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the 07:04 line twice. Once for the content. Once for what the kid had chosen to file it under. *Development* — the word a salvage crew used for a thing that hadn't gone wrong yet but was going to change shape. The kid had watched <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> leave in her field coat — the one she wore to jobs, not to the bench — and taken it further than <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had let himself take it.

The field coat. That was Bex's whole read, and it was correct, and Bex hadn't had to be told any part of it. You didn't put on the coat unless the world had already changed shape and you'd already decided to go meet it. The suspension request was the same logic wearing different clothes — *what job?* — the crew closing ranks around a thing they'd only guessed at, holding West Town because <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had walked out of it and that was reason enough. This log is the record. Meaning: whatever the boss decides, the crew has already voted.

He needed to catch <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> before she got clear of West Town and get a straight answer out of her about why the coat and why now — no more filing it under anything, his or the crew's. He folded the slip into his coat, unanswered, and went down to find the rest of his morning.

He ate at <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s at 08:00 — two bowls, schedule kept — and the work terminal chirped between the first and the second.

A posting on the standing contract. Not a task. Nobody had filed anything about the D-class; the client had found it on its own.

STANDING CONTRACT — ADDENDUM.
CLIENT ADVISES THE UNIT KEEPS A SHIFT. 0600 TO 2200.
CLIENT RESPECTS THIS.

No scope. No fee. No direction — only a machine somewhere noticing another machine keep its hours, and saying so. He wanted the addendum retracted before end of shift — a machine that watched him keep his hours was a machine that could file when he broke them, and he meant to file a clean refusal back up the chain and put the thing to rest. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> turned the terminal face-down and finished the bowl.

"You're thinking loud," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> said, setting the change beside him. She dropped a fish ball into his coat pocket without a word, and that was that.

"You're not going near—" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> started, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> set her cup down with a click that ended the sentence.

"Say the rest of that word and my rate doubles," she said. Not heated. The voice she used on a fastener that thought it was load-bearing. "The D-class runs a pre-2200 Axiom control bus. No remote interface — Axiom didn't trust radio, they were right, and they died before anyone retrofitted one. The bus has one physical maintenance spur, on the chassis, where I will be standing, because the alternative is nobody shuts this thing down and the city loses a neighborhood at the speed of careful chewing."

She turned the projection to face him. A schematic, hand-annotated in her tight engineer's print — she'd owned this before the job existed, the spur circled twice, the access window penciled beside it in her own hand: 90 sec, the number underlined like a load rating.

"I have wanted to talk to one of these since I was nine," she said. "You are not protecting me from it. You are buying me ninety seconds in front of it. That's the job, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>. Price it like one."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the schematic, and at his neighbor of four years in her field coat, and did the thing the moment called for.

"Standard rate," he said. "Yours is double. Specialist on site."

"Correct?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> asked.

"Correct," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> didn't smile, exactly. She made the face she made when a fastener came free without stripping — satisfaction filed somewhere below the surface, spent immediately on the next problem.

She keyed the crew channel. "Tell them the count."

The crew came together in thirty hours, because crews come together fast when the job is real and the pay is a joke. The job was real: get a nine-day-old D-class off its feet before it reached <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-c285-793e-bf21-a84522c9cf94">Auntie Som</entity>'s block, using a maintenance spur nobody had touched since <entity repo="corponation" guid="80a78887-98cf-4aa2-96fc-97c62a84fd21">Axiom</entity> Industrial stopped answering its own phones.

<entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa4-78db-9d54-bc054ba2a91b">Echo</entity> took eyes and comms — high ground, a voice in five skulls, never wrong about a sightline. <entity repo="character" guid="fe6ab919-9f3c-450b-aaf5-f24f84896521">Stash</entity> took transport: a flatbed he refused to explain, cases packed for every door in the brief.

The new hands came from the parts man and one of <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa4-78db-9d54-bc054ba2a91b">Echo</entity>'s old contacts. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> was a rigger off the lakefront cranes — big, slow-moving, maybe forty words a day, and she talked to suspended loads in the second person like they had opinions worth respecting. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-8f41-7b5d-8c7e-fc6b4e74dc25">Furnace</entity> was a demolition op with a thermal lance and the good cheer of a man whose tool settled most arguments; he'd burned scrap in the <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a5-7dfd-8f9f-91502211ef14">Ashgrave</entity> yards for a decade and knew the ground the D-class was standing on better than the D-class did.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-1757-74fd-8eb3-7e497fc642ab">Five</entity> of them and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>, in the back of <entity repo="character" guid="fe6ab919-9f3c-450b-aaf5-f24f84896521">Stash</entity>'s flatbed, on a contract worth less than the fuel it took to get there.

"Φ312," <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-8f41-7b5d-8c7e-fc6b4e74dc25">Furnace</entity> said, reading it off his cuff like a man checking the weather. "Seven shares, once <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> takes her double. That's forty-four Φ and change a head."

"Correct," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, not looking up from the schematic.

"For a job that puts one of us on the hull of a live demolition automaton."

"Correct."

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-8f41-7b5d-8c7e-fc6b4e74dc25">Furnace</entity> grinned like she'd told him something good. "Just wanted it said out loud once."

<entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa4-78db-9d54-bc054ba2a91b">Echo</entity>, from the cab, didn't turn around. "Sightline on the maintenance spur's clean from the water tower. I've had eyes on that D-class for six hours. I know every step it's taken since Tuesday." A pause, the kind that usually didn't happen in her voice. "It changed its gait an hour ago. Shorter stride, same chassis. I don't have a reason for that yet."

"Find one," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said.

"I will," <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa4-78db-9d54-bc054ba2a91b">Echo</entity> said, too fast, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> heard it — the half-second where *never wrong about a sightline* had to work to stay true.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity>, from the flatbed rail, said nothing at all. She was looking at the schematic upside down, reading the load lines the way other people read a room.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat with his ribs against the flatbed's wheel well and did the math the crew wasn't saying out loud: fifty-two Q a head, six people, one machine that had never been told to stop, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> standing ninety seconds from its chassis because a woman named <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-c285-793e-bf21-a84522c9cf94">Auntie Som</entity> had a biscuit tin and nowhere else to send it.

"Nobody's here for the money," he said.

"No," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> agreed, still reading the schematic. "We're here because it's solvable."

They walked the eaten blocks first, because <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> wanted to see its work.

The thing was tidy. That was the part that climbed into <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> and stayed. Nine days of rubble stood in sorted piles at even intervals — ferrous, mineral, organics — each pile compacted square, each street swept after, the lamppost bases unscrewed and laid out in rows like cutlery. No fire, no scatter. The machine had moved through the neighborhood the way a knife moves through paper, and the paper had stayed where it fell. A city block taken apart with the intent to account for every piece.

Tidy meant it knew what it was doing. That was the part that made a man go quiet.

In the middle of the fourth block the piles stopped mattering, because the machine was there.

Eleven feet at the shoulder. Four legs, two boom arms, a hull of sintered gray printed in one piece — no plates, no rivets, no panel lines, no seams at all. Low black discs studded the hull every foot, and around each disc the rain steamed faintly off the surface. It sat clean in the yard it had made, three sensor clusters rotating on a slow axis, reading its own work.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> walked straight to it and stopped three meters short.

"Arc-fence," she said. "Anti-tamper. Capacitive plates — the whole hull is one big charge bank. Anything conductive touches the skin, the skin touches back. Forty thousand volts of touches back." She traced the geometry in the air the way other people read a face, her hands moving through the space around the hull without ever closing the distance. "Axiom-spec, pre-2200. Their insurance policy. Nobody opens this thing without authorization. Nobody *can*."

She looked at <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>'s saya, then at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>.

"Your sword is a key for doors, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>. That thing has no doors. No seams, no cable runs, nothing routed on the surface — Axiom buried it all a foot deep in the structure. There's nothing on that hull for an edge to mean. <entity repo="material" guid="06149735-8358-b741-7e90-8e1e182330c8">Steel</entity> and carbon, both conductive. You touch it, you're not cutting, you're grounding it. It'll cook your neuretics inside your skull, and the burn scar will be the shape of your own blade."

"So I don't touch it?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"You don't touch it." She was already moving again, reading the chassis from a new angle, calculating the precise distance between where a body would have to stand and where the current would be waiting. "Tonight your job is everything that isn't it."

It kept a schedule. The D-class worked a shift, 0600 to 2200. At 0300 it walked back to the dead Axiom yard and docked against a transformer pylon to charge. It had done that every night for nine days. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, quietly, that it had probably been doing it since 2196 — until somebody powered it down mid-rotation and walked away.

"So we take the dock window," she said. "Tonight, 0300, while it's tethered and blind. We get onto the spur, splice the bus, and pull whatever it's still running before it wakes up. That's the job."

She had the schematic pinned to a steel plate, a work light clamped above it, the crew gathered in the half-dark like they were looking at a corpse. The maintenance spur was marked in yellow — actual highlighter, on printed paper, the kind of analog that made <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s neuretics itch.

"It docks, the arc-fence drops to maintenance levels, the spur goes live," she said. "Axiom units safe themselves for service. The spur is on the hull. Conductive. While the fence is live, I touch it, I'm not getting back up. When it drops it's not off — dropped. Residual charge in the plates. Still enough to hurt. Not enough to kill if I'm not stupid about it. Ninety seconds on the spur, handshake with the bus, find out why it's awake."

"And if the handshake goes wrong?" Echo asked.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> didn't answer right away. She was still looking at the schematic, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched her thumb stop moving over the glass.

"Then I'm standing on a live hull with the fence back up before I can get clear," she said. "So it doesn't go wrong."

"That's not an answer," Echo said. "That's a hope with math on it."

"It's a *coupling seal*," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, and something in her voice flattened out, went procedural, the register she used for things she didn't want looked at too long. "Thirty-year format. The bank needs a bleed cycle or it burns itself out. Same drop, same time, every night. I've read the Axiom service architecture since I was nine years old, in a room that didn't have anything else in it. I know this bus better than the engineers who scrapped it. If I say ninety seconds, it's ninety seconds."

"How many of these have you actually stood on," <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-8f41-7b5d-8c7e-fc6b4e74dc25">Furnace</entity> said. Not unkind. Just asking.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>, half a beat too long.

"None," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said. "There aren't any left to stand on. That's the point."

Nobody said anything to that. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> kept reading the load lines upside down, reading the machine's weight the way other people read a room. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e2-727a-be75-32648e8aaa47">Rain</entity> ticked off the hull discs and steamed away, foot by foot, all the way down the block.

"Then it objects," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, "and the five of you get to be more interesting than I am."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at her — four years of knowing her face for what a fastener coming loose without stripping looked like — and saw the thing underneath it for the first time: not confidence. Arithmetic she'd run so many times alone that she'd stopped being able to tell the difference between *certain* and *practiced.*

"Ninety seconds," he said. "I'll be standing where I can reach you before the fence comes back."

"You'll be standing where I tell you," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, already turning back to the schematic, folding it with both hands, the kind of careful that meant she'd folded it a thousand times before, muscle memory older than the job. "Because if you're where you think you should be, you're in my blast radius when this goes right."

The docking cycle showed on Echo's feed at 0247. Thirteen minutes.

It docked. The boom arms folded. The black discs on the hull dimmed one by one. A contactor closed somewhere inside, and the transformer pylon began, gently, to sing.

"Maintenance state," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said, already moving. "<entity repo="archetype" guid="019d6143-a56e-7633-bbad-bed2a04b007d">Fence</entity> is down to a tickle. Ninety seconds. Count me."

She crossed the yard at a walk — running hands shake — stepped over <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a4-71f6-b46a-94ef8cb2348f">Arcturus</entity>'s cone, and put her bare hand flat on the hull. It was the way she put it between <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s shoulder blades before she trusted a readout.

"Hello, you absurd old thing," she said, too quiet for the channel, and found the spur. <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaf8-73f2-b86b-bbc32205c8f9">Splice</entity> gun. Bus contact. The handshake initiating.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> counted from the pylon, three meters clear, because <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had drawn a perimeter on the schematic and his name was outside it. The disconnect hung at his shoulder — a lever the size of his forearm, painted a yellow that had stopped meaning anything, labeled in a font retired before he was born, welded now into its own rust. Supposed to stay locked. Nothing in the Axiom yards stayed locked once you knew where to look.

The whole yard counted. The handshake chattered in her earpiece — Axiom bus protocol running both ways for the first time in thirty years. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched the discs stay dim, maintenance-level, second by second, while her fingers worked the coupling.

At second forty-one of ninety, a power flicker rolled through the dead grid. Not a flicker. A stutter — the kind of dropout that shouldn't happen on a dedicated charge circuit, the kind that makes lights blink three blocks away. He felt it climb the disconnect lever and into his palms before his brain caught what it meant. The pylon's note wavered a quarter-tone. And the D-class's watchdog, which had kept this machine alive through three decades of abandonment, made the only decision a watchdog knows.

Every disc on the hull lit at once.

"Off the chassis—" Echo said, and the machine stood up out of its dock with <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s cable still live, and the night went to work.

The machine's boom arms came up like it was waking from a bad dream.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved. Not toward <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>—toward the east catwalk, the one that ran above the charging collar, the one that gave him sight line on the transformer pylon's main breaker. Thirty years this machine had been docked here. Thirty years it had learned the geometry of its own charging cycle. Thirty years it had learned what "safe" felt like.

Now it was redefining safe.

The boom arms rotated. Not searching. Executing. The machine pivoted on its front two legs and the world lit up like someone had switched on a sun inside a <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-ab07-73ce-97e4-b3934d12c0d9">tin can</entity>.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"I see it. Eighty seconds to full charge cascade—"

The machine's chassis rose six inches off the dock. Not standing up. Preparing. The arc-fence hummed from a subsonic whisper to a frequency <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt in his teeth.

"Forty," <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> called. The container hadn't moved. He was holding it steady on released cables, waiting for the word that would never come now.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> covered the last of the catwalk in a sprint that ate concrete. The metal was wet and cold under his boots, the grating ringing at every stride. He could see the transformer pylon from here—see the black maintenance box bolted to its base, see the manual disconnect lever that should have been painted red but was just black like everything else in this part of the city. Should have been accessible. Should have been labeled. Should have been a lot of things.

The arc-fence came online in sequence. Disc by disc, the hull lit—not a flicker but a progression, deliberate as a countdown, the capacitive plates charging in cascade. The rain around the machine stopped steaming and started boiling.

The D-class's legs locked rigid.

Cold, the way she made them when she knew a man wouldn't touch them right away — the broth already carrying its thin skin, the sign that time had passed and had cost something to pass.

The supplemental had no answer in it that wasn't another question — why a thing with nobody left to obey had stopped at a dead crossing and waited out a light that would never change. He broke the skin on the broth with his chopsticks and read it a second time, slower, the way a man reads a thing he already knows but needs to hold. It gave him nothing the first reading hadn't. He set it aside with everything else he didn't have an answer for, and started on his second bowl.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> filled his water without being asked, and went back to setting clean bowls out along the counter in a line — small, practiced movements, morning service, the same as the morning before the machine woke and the same as tomorrow. Outside the glass the street was deciding to be a street again: freight starting up, the fringe kids already out. The noodles were still warm.

A week later, the laundry came.

Somebody on the fringe ran the first line from a ground-floor window to the D-class's folded foreleg. By the weekend there were nine lines — sheets and work shirts and a yellowed wedding tablecloth drying in the lake wind off thirty-five feet of the tidiest demolition in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> history. Kids dared each other to slap the dead arc-fence discs and ran away screaming on the inhale. A vendor moved her cart into its shade on hot afternoons.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> rode past it once, the long way, wanting only to know whether it had held — whether the thing he had made of that block was still the thing he had intended. He would take one slow pass, read the piles against his memory of how he'd left them, and settle it: proof the order stuck without him standing over it, or proof he'd have to come back and stand over it again. His palm wore his own grip in scar tissue. He did not slow down. He did not need to.

The residents had drawn an invisible line around the flatbed and the machine and the work that mattered, and they were holding it. The D-class was folded in the center, knees and shoulders down, the way something sleeps when it knows it won't wake up. The salvage had settled into custody the way a number settles once it's been counted in front of everyone — you didn't build machines like it anymore, not out here, not since the yards started building them to fail on schedule so somebody had to buy the next one. This one had been built to work. Not to be replaced. Not to be profitable. Just to work. And the street had decided, without a vote, that the version of the story where restraint paid was the true one, and it wasn't giving the ending back.

The piles stayed sorted. Nobody touched the piles.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> had ridden home in the coat that day and stayed there since, unspent.
